extra.candidate_title: GPT-6 and Intelligent UI for everyone
extra.source_text: October 7, 2026 Product Release GPT‑6 and Intelligent UI for everyone Loading… Share Last month we introduced the first GPT‑6 models for paid customers and today we're bringing that next generation of intelligence to more people with a new GPT‑6 model built for more than 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week. GPT‑6 in ChatGPT introduces Intelligent UI, a new capability that allows ChatGPT to answer quickly with fully interactive user interfaces that make everyday answers more visual, make learning complex topics easier and that can quickly create a tool to solve a task right in the moment. break down the design of a 7‑speed bike All Frame Wheels Drivetrain Brakes Cockpit 7‑Speed Bicycle 7‑Speed Bicycle 7‑Speed Bicycle Chat Images Intelligent UI A 7‑speed bicycle brings together a frame, handlebars, wheels and hand-operated brakes. Seven gears let the rider adjust pedaling effort as the drivetrain turns effort into motion. Upright bars guide the steering, gears vary the effort, and hand brakes control the pace. Five connected systems The frame carries the rider; the drivetrain turns effort into motion. Select a system to explore its role. A strong foundation Two triangles connect the saddle, steering and pedals. The fork holds the front wheel and turns with the bars. Made to keep rolling Spokes connect each hub to its rim and support the rider. The tires surround the rims and grip the ground. Seven ways to move The pedals turn the chain, driving the rear wheel. Seven gears let the rider adjust pedaling effort for climbs, flats and descents. Control at the rim Hand levers pull cables that bring the brake pads against the rims, turning a squeeze into controlled slowing. Steering and support The handlebars and stem steer the front wheel. The saddle and seatpost support the rider and set the sitting position. break down the design of a 7‑speed bike Chat Chat 7‑Speed Bicycle Side view of a 7-speed bicycle with five connected systems All Frame Wheels Drivetrain Brakes Cockpit A 7‑speed bicycle brings together a frame, handlebars, wheels and hand-operated brakes. Seven gears let the rider adjust pedaling effort as the drivetrain turns effort into motion. Introducing Intelligent UI We’ve trained GPT‑6 to compose responses using text, visuals and interactive elements, choosing how they fit together based on your question. With Intelligent UI, responses can include graphics, tappable buttons, forms, charts, and interactive experiences you can use directly in your conversation. The format depends on what you’re asking. A comparison might work best side by side. An explanation might be easier to understand through an interactive diagram. And when a simple text answer is the most useful response, ChatGPT can give you that. More visual responses to everyday questions ChatGPT can make a plan easier to follow by showing how it fits together. The timing for a Sunday roast can sit alongside the recipe, or the stops on a road trip can appear on a map, with notes on what’s worth a detour. Learn complex topics more easily Visual and interactive explanations let you explore how something works, change an input to see what happens, or work through a problem step by step. Create interactive experiences just by asking You can also ask ChatGPT to create a tool for the task at hand, such as a calculator to explore how savings could grow, a bill splitter for dinner with friends, or a game you can play in the conversation. How Intelligent UI works With Intelligent UI, we gave GPT‑6 the freedom to create the most useful interface for each question, while keeping the experience fast and familiar across web and mobile. We built a library of native, streamable components, along with a compiler that processes the interface as the model generates it. The library gives each response a familiar design foundation while leaving the model room to decide how the pieces fit together. The compiler allows the interface to appear progressively as the model generates it, without waiting for the entire response to be complete. We expanded our training methods to help the model make thoughtful decisions about content, layout, visuals, and interaction. This included evaluating the interfaces it creates for clarity, usefulness, and completeness. GPT‑6 learned to use the component library and make good design decisions, including how to organize information clearly, when to use interactivity, and when a simple text response is enough. There's still work ahead to improve the model's design judgment and expand what it can create, but Intelligent UI marks a significant shift in how people interact with ChatGPT. Instead of fitting every question into the same conversational format, ChatGPT can combine UI, data, and actions to create entirely new ways for people to explore, understand, and interact with information. Frontier Intelligence – delivered more quickly With GPT‑6, we’re also making it possible for ChatGPT to begin answering while it continues to think. GPT‑5.6 Instant GPT‑6 Instant With the introduction of reasoning models, users could get help with much harder problems, but had to wait for the model to finish thinking before getting an answer. Now, ChatGPT can interleave thinking with answering. We trained it to take into account the user’s waiting time and progressively compose an answer using its knowledge and findings up to that point. It learned to build answers across multiple partial responses, each adding useful information without unnecessary filler, while keeping the full answer as cohesive and factual as one written all at once. In an internal evaluation of high-value, everyday agentic tasks, GPT‑6 Extra High is able to begin answering in the same amount of time as GPT‑5.6 Medium while achieving a better overall score than GPT‑5.6 Extra High. For questions that need web search, GPT‑6 Instant starts answering 44% sooner, on average, than GPT‑5.6 Instant. GPT‑6 also improves the quality of answers that require web search. It makes better decisions about when to look something up and more reliably finds information that supports its answer. In an internal evaluation of difficult problems, GPT‑6 correctly addressed the key aspect of the user’s question more often than GPT‑5.6. Deploying GPT‑6 safely As we bring more intelligent AI to more people, we work to improve how it recognizes real-world risks, how honestly it responds, and how well it respects the limits that people set. GPT‑6 makes progress in each of these areas, building on several of Astra’s safety advances to better resist attempts to bypass its safety training, follow safeguards, and be clearer about what it can and can’t do relative to GPT‑5.6 Sol. We updated its safety training based on lessons from real-world use to strengthen protections against high-risk misuse involving cyberattacks, biological threats, and violence. In adversarial testing, GPT‑6 showed stronger resistance to attempts to bypass its safety training, particularly attacks that adapt across multiple turns. GPT‑6 is also trained to respond safely in higher-risk scenarios while avoiding unnecessary refusals of harmless requests. This includes using conversation history and relevant context to recognize risks that may not be apparent from a single prompt. We ran alignment evaluations throughout training, assessing honesty and responses to safety restrictions. GPT‑6 is better at recognizing and communicating the limits of its own capabilities, including when it lacks the information or tools needed to answer. More detail on the results and our review is available in the system card ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Availability GPT‑6 with Intelligent UI starts rolling out globally to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise tiers today in the Chat tab. Starting tomorrow, the rollout expands to Free and Go tiers. Enterprise availability depends on workplace admin settings. GPT‑6 in ChatGPT is powered by GPT‑6 Sol for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise tiers, and GPT‑6 Luna for Free and Go tiers. Both are tuned for everyday conversation. This update applies to the Chat experience in ChatGPT. The models powering Work and Codex are not changing as part of this release. What comes next Our mission is to deliver the benefits of artificial general intelligence safely to all of humanity. GPT‑6 brings our latest advances in intelligence to the more than 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT every week. Intelligent UI is a step toward a ChatGPT that can shape an interface around what you’re trying to do. Over time, we want ChatGPT to create more of the interfaces people need for everyday tasks. You should be able to describe what you want to accomplish and work with an experience built around it. For decades, people have had to learn how to use software, navigating fixed interfaces designed around particular tasks. We believe the future will be different. Instead of people adapting to software, software will adapt to people. 2026 ChatGPT Author OpenAI Keep reading View all Helping teens learn, plan, and shape the future of AI Product Oct 7, 2026 Building advertising for the way people use AI Product Oct 5, 2026 A practical guide to building with GPT-6 Product Oct 2, 2026

tools.headline: Codex CLI 0.157.0 starts a background daemon by default, and users want it off
tools.summary: After 0.157.0, opening Codex can start a background process that keeps running after you close the window and checks for updates hourly.
tools.why_it_matters: The background updater can restart the backend and kill active turns, so a long Codex run can get cut off without warning.
tools.for_builders: Run codex features disable daemon_auto_start, then codex app-server daemon stop to stop it.

extra.candidate_title: Codex CLI installs a persistent, self-updating background daemon by default
extra.source_text: CLI: make daemon_auto_start opt-in — a persistent, self-updating background daemon shouldn't be the default #48195 New issue Copy link New issue Copy link Open Open CLI: make daemon_auto_start opt-in — a persistent, self-updating background daemon shouldn't be the default #48195 Copy link Labels CLI Issues related to the Codex CLI Issues related to the Codex CLI app-server Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces enhancement New feature or request New feature or request Description Yihua-Liu-1997 opened on Sep 25, 2026 Issue body actions What variant of Codex are you using? CLI — 0.157.0, installed via npm install -g @openai/codex , Linux (WSL2) What feature would you like to see? Please make daemon_auto_start opt-in (default false ) for the CLI , or at least ask once before turning it on. Since 0.157.0, just opening an interactive codex session: Starts a persistent background daemon ( codex app-server --managed-daemon ). It runs in its own session with no TTY and keeps running after every Codex window is closed (reparented to PID 1) until codex app-server daemon stop or a reboot. Copies the whole platform package (~374 MB: codex , codex-code-mode-host , bundled bwrap / zsh / rg ) into ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/releases/<version>/ — byte-identical to what npm had just installed — and runs the daemon from that copy. From then on the backend's version is decoupled from the CLI version I installed with my package manager. Starts a detached updater ( codex app-server daemon pid-update-loop ) that checks for updates 5 minutes after start and then hourly, downloads new releases and restarts the backend (which can kill active turns, see app-server daemon: auto-update force-kills active turns after a 60s drain budget, and cannot be disabled #40969 ). Pins the environment of whichever session happened to start it. I launch Codex through a wrapper that sets HTTPS_PROXY per invocation; the daemon keeps the first session's proxy variables and its outbound connections go through that proxy, whatever later sessions are launched with. Hooks in --remote mode receive the daemon's cwd, not the session's #42457 and Hooks spawned by the app-server daemon cannot identify the client terminal, breaking terminal-targeting hooks #37537 (daemon cwd / terminal instead of the session's) look like the same root cause. For a CLI, the least surprising default is that the backend lives and dies with the window, runs the binary I installed, and doesn't update itself in the background. A shared, self-updating daemon makes sense for Remote Control / the desktop app, so it would be fine to enable it there, or when the user explicitly runs codex app-server daemon start / bootstrap . If it stays on by default, please at least: exit an auto-started daemon when its last client disconnects; not copy/self-update when the CLI was installed by a package manager (npm/brew/pacman) — run the installed binary instead ( Support externally managed app-server daemon executables #41188 , npm update leaves app-server on old version, but daemon update/restart refuse recovery #46468 , Codex 0.157.0 no longer starts with the Arch Linux package unless --no-daemon is used #48050 ). Additional information Bug found while turning it off: codex app-server daemon stop stops the app-server but leaves the pid-update-loop updater running (still alive 70 s later, had to kill it manually). Workaround I'm using: codex features disable daemon_auto_start codex app-server daemon stop pkill -f ' app-server daemon pid-update-loop ' # not stopped by `daemon stop` rm -rf ~ /.codex/packages/app-server-daemon With the flag off, a new TUI session no longer spawns a daemon. tools.headline: Docker Agent: build and run AI helpers from one YAML file
tools.summary: Docker Agent lets you define a team of AI helpers in a short YAML config, with no code required.
tools.why_it_matters: You can give an assistant web search through a ready-made tool and run it from your terminal without writing a program.
tools.for_builders: Install Docker Desktop (4.63+), which pre-installs the docker-agent plugin, then run: docker agent run agent.yaml

extra.source_text: 🤖 Docker Agent 🤖 Build, run, and share AI agents with a declarative YAML config, rich tool ecosystem, and multi-agent orchestration. What is Docker Agent? docker-agent lets you create and run intelligent AI agents that collaborate to solve complex problems — no code required. docker-agent is a docker CLI plugin and can be run with docker agent . Define agents in YAML, give them tools, and let them work. agents : root : model : openai/gpt-5-mini description : A helpful AI assistant instruction : | You are a knowledgeable assistant that helps users with various tasks. Be helpful, accurate, and concise in your responses. toolsets : - type : mcp ref : docker:duckduckgo docker agent run agent.yaml Key Features Multi-agent architecture — Create teams of specialized agents that delegate tasks automatically Rich tool ecosystem — Built-in tools + any MCP server (local, remote, or Docker-based) AI provider agnostic — OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Mistral, xAI, Docker Model Runner , and more YAML configuration — Declarative, versionable, shareable Advanced reasoning — Built-in think, todo, and memory tools RAG — Pluggable retrieval with BM25, embeddings, hybrid search, and reranking Package & share — Push agents to any OCI registry, pull and run them anywhere Install Docker Desktop (4.63+) — docker-agent CLI plugin is pre-installed. Just run docker agent . Homebrew — brew install docker-agent . Run docker-agent directly or symlink the binary to ~/.docker/cli-plugins/docker-agent and run docker agent . Binary releases — Download from GitHub Releases . Symlink the docker-agent binary to ~/.docker/cli-plugins/docker-agent to be able to use docker agent , or use docker-agent directly. Set at least one API key (or use Docker Model Runner for local models): export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... # or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GOOGLE_API_KEY, etc. See Set Up a Model for the full walkthrough of both paths (cloud API key or local model). Quick Start # Run the default agent docker agent run # Run from an OCI registry docker agent run myorg/agent:tag # Generate a new agent interactively docker agent new # Run your own config docker agent run agent.yaml More examples in the examples/ directory. Documentation 📖 Full documentation Installation · Set Up a Model · Quick Start Agents · Models · Tools · Multi-Agent Configuration Reference TUI · CLI · MCP Mode · RAG Model Providers · Docker Model Runner Contributing Read the Contributing guide to get started. We use docker-agent to build docker-agent : docker agent run ./golang_developer.yaml Telemetry We collect anonymous usage data to improve the tool. See Telemetry . extra.description: An agent skill for creating detailed, interactive isometric illustrations of real-world machines and complex systems. Generates polished SVGs with optional WebGL shaders and 3D effects.
extra.source_text:
An agent skill for creating detailed, interactive isometric illustrations of real-world machines and complex systems. Generates polished SVGs with optional WebGL shaders and 3D effects.

Anatomy

A Claude skill that explains an idea by building it as a real, working object.
Also runs in OpenCode and Codex.
Crafted, interactive isometric figures with many small precise parts, in SVG, WebGL and 3D.

   

Quick start · Gallery · What it makes · Install · Usage · Examples · How it works · Limits

examples/raptor-engine, light theme, firing. The engine and stand are SVG; the plume is a WebGL shader in the same isometric camera.

--- Ask Claude for a figure that explains a technical idea, and Anatomy has it invent a physical thing whose working *is* the concept. A cache key that skips work when nothing changed becomes a pin-tumbler lock that only turns when every pin matches. One GPU context serving many canvases becomes a gantry plotter whose single print head visits 16 wells. Then Claude builds that thing out of dozens of small, solid, shaded parts, puts it in a framed card with a title, a hint and a live readout, makes it move calmly under the pointer and the keyboard, and checks its own work by zooming in on every joint. Every number the figure shows comes from the same small model that moves its parts. ## Quick start ```sh npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a claude-code ``` Then, in Claude Code: ```text /anatomy explain how a token bucket rate limiter works, interactive ``` For OpenCode or Codex, swap the agent: `-a opencode` or `-a codex`. OpenCode takes the same `/anatomy` command; in Codex, type `$anatomy`. That's it. No API keys and nothing to `npm install`: the kit uses only Node's built-in modules. ## Gallery
raptor-engine: hover to take it apart into 11 assemblies. An audit proves that no pipe passes through anything, at rest, apart and in every frame between. ripple-tank: SVG apparatus over two WebGL layers (lamp light and caustics on the paper, reflections in the water) driven by a dispersion and optics model.
turning-dial: the 3D mode (beta). About 90 parts are re-projected and re-shaded every frame as you drag the dial. dial-indicator: the smallest example, about 300 lines. Hover to slide the carriage; the needle reads each block.
Every screenshot is the light theme of a page in [`examples/`](examples), captured with the skill's own [`scripts/capture.mjs`](scripts/capture.mjs) and [`scripts/drive.mjs`](scripts/drive.mjs). The built pages are committed: open any `.html` in `examples/` to try it. ## What it makes Three kinds of figure. All three share one kit, one camera and one set of craft rules. | Kind | What it is | Example | |---|---|---| | **SVG** | The core. Solid isometric parts with four-tone shading, painted back to front, in a card with a live readout and eased motion. It ships as a standalone HTML page, a lone `.svg` file with its styles embedded, or React/Next.js components. | `dial-indicator`, `desk-computer`, `arcade-cabinet`, `test-rig` | | **SVG + WebGL** | For what lines can't draw: fire, exhaust, water, caustics, lamp light, glow, steam. The shader runs in a canvas between a back and a front SVG, in the figure's own isometric camera, so it sits inside the drawing. The SVG still reads without WebGL. | `raptor-engine`, `ripple-tank` | | **3D** beta | Parts that turn in true 3D: a dial or turntable that spins, fingers that flex, a piece that breaks off and falls. The moving parts are re-projected and re-shaded by the kit's own rules every frame; the rest of the figure stays static art. | `turning-dial` | Each figure is light or dark. Light is the theme the skill designs for first, shaders included. ## Install Anatomy is a standard [Agent Skill](https://agentskills.io): a folder with a `SKILL.md` at its root. This repository is that folder. Pick one way in: | | Command | Installs to | |---|---|---| | **skills CLI**, for you (Claude Code) | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a claude-code` | `~/.claude/skills/anatomy` | | **skills CLI**, for you (Antigravity) | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a antigravity` | `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy` | | **skills CLI**, for you (OpenCode) | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a opencode` | `~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy` | | **skills CLI**, for you (Codex) | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a codex` | `~/.agents/skills/anatomy` | | **skills CLI**, for one project | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy` | `.claude/skills/anatomy` for Claude Code, `.agents/skills/anatomy` for Antigravity, OpenCode and Codex | | **git**, for you (Claude Code) | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git ~/.claude/skills/anatomy` | `~/.claude/skills/anatomy` | | **git**, for you (Antigravity) | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git ~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy` | `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy` | | **git**, for you (OpenCode) | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git ~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy` | `~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy` | | **git**, for you (Codex) | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git ~/.agents/skills/anatomy` | `~/.agents/skills/anatomy` | | **git**, for one project | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git .claude/skills/anatomy` | `.claude/skills/anatomy` (Claude Code and OpenCode) or `.agents/skills/anatomy` (Antigravity, OpenCode and Codex) | | **Download**, no git | see below | any of the folders above |
With the skills CLI
The [`skills`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) CLI finds the `SKILL.md` at the root of this repository and installs it as `anatomy`. By default it installs into the current project and asks which agents to set up. `-g` installs it for your user, and `-a claude-code` sets up Claude Code only. Use `-a antigravity`, `-a opencode` or `-a codex` for Antigravity, OpenCode or Codex only. The CLI copies the whole repository, examples included (about 10 MB). It needs a recent Node.js: version 1.7.1 of the CLI asks for 22.20 or later.
With git
Clone the repository into one of the skill folders, so that `SKILL.md` ends up at `/anatomy/SKILL.md`. For Claude Code use `~/.claude/skills/anatomy` or `.claude/skills/anatomy`. For Antigravity use `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy` or `.agents/skills/anatomy`. For OpenCode use `~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy` or `.opencode/skills/anatomy`; OpenCode also reads the Claude Code and `.agents` folders. For Codex use `~/.agents/skills/anatomy` or `.agents/skills/anatomy`. For a project install, commit the folder so your team gets it too. To update later, `git pull` inside that folder.
Download, without git
[Download the ZIP](https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy/archive/refs/heads/main.zip), unpack it, rename the folder from `anatomy-main` to `anatomy`, and move it into `~/.claude/skills/` (Claude Code), `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/` (Antigravity), `~/.config/opencode/skills/` (OpenCode) or `~/.agents/skills/` (Codex). Or in one line on macOS or Linux: ```sh mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/anatomy && curl -L https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy/archive/refs/heads/main.tar.gz | tar -xz --strip-components=1 -C ~/.claude/skills/anatomy ``` For Antigravity, OpenCode or Codex, put the same files in `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy`, `~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy` or `~/.agents/skills/anatomy`: ```sh mkdir -p ~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy && curl -L https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy/archive/refs/heads/main.tar.gz | tar -xz --strip-components=1 -C ~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy ``` ```sh mkdir -p ~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy && curl -L https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy/archive/refs/heads/main.tar.gz | tar -xz --strip-components=1 -C ~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy ```
Claude Code picks up new skills in a running session. If the `skills` folder itself did not exist when the session started, run `/reload-skills`. Antigravity and OpenCode list it as `/anatomy` in their chat; restart if it does not show. Codex lists it under `/skills` and runs it with `$anatomy`; restart Codex if it does not show.

extra.source_text: Let your AI agents paint big arrows, boxes and text on your Mac screen. One CLI, click-through, gone by itself. Skill for Claude Code and Codex. MIT. # Let your AI agents paint big arrows, boxes and text on your screen **big-arrow-on-the-screen** (`bigarrow`) is a macOS command-line tool, plus a skill for Claude Code and Codex, that draws an arrow and a sign on top of every window. Clicks go through, your keyboard focus stays put, and the arrow removes itself. MIT licensed. [![CI](https://github.com/franzenzenhofer/big-arrow-on-the-screen/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/franzenzenhofer/big-arrow-on-the-screen/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) ![A real macOS desktop, Hacker News of 2014-06-10 in Chrome, nine bigarrow arrows in nine colours from every side: same since 2007, already argued in 2014, not a lurker? log in, the article is in here, remember me? (Firefox 30), nothing. nothing changed. (a spiral, going round in circles), 20,000 devs 40,000 opinions, finally a bigger arrow, 12 years later: still no consensus](docs/images/hero-hn.png) [Real apps](#real-apps-real-use-cases) · [Copy & paste](#copy--paste) · [What is it for?](#what-is-this-actually-for) · [Install](#install) · [Commands](#the-three-commands-an-agent-needs) · [Looks](#looks) · [Creative arrows](#creative-arrows) · [Starred by](#starred-by) · [FAQ](#faq) · [How we know it works](#how-we-know-it-works) · [For agents](#for-agents-and-the-humans-who-configure-them) · [Plan](#plan-decisions-research) · [Prior art](#prior-art-and-thanks) · [License](#license) > Your AI agent can refactor a monorepo, write a migration and explain monads, but when it needs you to click one button it prints *"please click Allow in the dialog"* into a terminal you are not looking at. `bigarrow` gives it a finger. ![bigarrow pointing at a dialog's Allow button](docs/images/demo.gif) ```bash bigarrow point --element "Allow" --app "System Settings" --text "Franz, click Allow: Ghostty may control your Mac" ``` One transparent window above everything, on every display and every Space. Drawing needs **no macOS permission at all**. One Swift binary: no daemon, no menu-bar icon, no account, no telemetry, and, we checked twice, no AI inside. It is an arrow. ## Real apps, real use cases Real apps on a real Mac (macOS 27), the real `bigarrow`, staged by `scripts/real-scenes.sh`. ### macOS Desktop & Dock: stop "click wallpaper to show desktop" ![An agent walks a human through the most complained-about Mac setting since 2023: one click on the wallpaper and every window flees; then 1. The apple. Yes, the fruit. 2. System Settings. Where settings go to hide. 3. Desktop & Dock. Not Wallpaper. Not Displays. This one. 4. Scroll. Further. It's always further. 5. 'Show desktop'. Nothing to do with Stage Manager. 6. 'Only in Stage Manager' means 'off'. Obviously. Then the wallpaper click: Nothing happens. Bliss.](docs/images/real/wallpaper.gif) ["The most annoying change in Mac update history"](https://www.imore.com/mac/macos/macos-sonoma-click-to-reveal-desktop-turn-off), fixed in six arrows ([MP4](docs/videos/wallpaper.mp4)). ### System Settings: grant a permission ![System Settings, Device Control and Data Access: a green arrow with a close button, Franz, switch this on: Terminal may control your Mac, and an orange zigzag ring on the plus button: Not in the list? Plus. Then find it.](docs/images/real/settings.png) ```bash open "x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.preference.security?Privacy_Accessibility" bigarrow start --element Terminal_Toggle --app "System Settings" \ --text "Franz, switch this on: Terminal may control your Mac" --from right --color green --close-button bigarrow start --element Add --role button --app "System Settings" \ --text "Not in the list? Plus. Then find it." --from bottom-right --style ring --color orange --shape zigzag --size S ``` ### Keynote: a three-step how-to ![Keynote: a purple ring, 1. Click Animate; an orange box, 2. Add an Effect; a teal zigzag on Play, 3. Press play. Bask in the applause.](docs/images/real/keynote.png) ```bash bigarrow start --element Animate --app Keynote --role radiobutton --text "1. Click Animate" --from right \ --style ring --color purple bigarrow start --element "Add an Effect" --app Keynote --text "2. Add an Effect" --from right \ --style box --corners sharp --color "#FF9F0A" --shape straight bigarrow start --element Play --app Keynote --role button --text "3. Press play. Bask in the applause." \ --from top --color teal --shape zigzag --size S ``` ### Print dialog: helping Mom save a PDF ![TextEdit print dialog: a pink arrow, Mom, click PDF, then Save as PDF, and a small black one on Cancel: Not this one, Mom](docs/images/real/print.png) ```bash bigarrow start --element PDF --role button --app TextEdit \ --text "Mom, click PDF, then Save as PDF" --from bottom --color pink --border white-black bigarrow start --element Cancel --role button --app TextEdit \ --text "Not this one, Mom" --from bottom-right --color black --size S ``` ### Chrome: the right tab out of 14 ![Chrome, three windows, 14 tabs, a big indigo sign: It's this tab, not the other 13](docs/images/real/chrome.png) ```bash bigarrow start --app "Google Chrome:Sourdough" --element "Sourdough - Wikipedia" --role radiobutton \ --text "It's this tab, not the other 13" --from top --shape zigzag --color "#5856D6" --size L ``` `--app "App:tab title"` raises the window and selects the tab first. ### Finder: "no, the other grid icon" ![Finder: a black ring on the icon view button, Not this one, and a green box on the Group button: No, the other grid icon. This one.](docs/images/real/finder.png) ```bash bigarrow start --element "icon view" --role radiobutton --app Finder \ --text "Not this one" --from top-left --style ring --color black --size S bigarrow start --element Group --role menubutton --app Finder \ --text "No, the other grid icon. This one." --from top --style box --color green ``` ### A real guide: allow screen recording The whole guide as a 6-page PDF, every screenshot an arrow an agent drew. [Download the PDF](docs/guides/allow-screen-recording/how-to-allow-screen-recording-on-a-mac.pdf) or [read it here](docs/guides/allow-screen-recording/README.md). ## Copy & paste `{{value}}` in the sign becomes a copy button. Click, paste. ![A made-up sign-in page asks for a PIN; a blue arrow with a yellow border points at the empty field: Franz, copy & paste the PIN 482913 here, the PIN on a yellow copy button](docs/images/real/copy-pin.png) ![The same moment after the click: the copy icon is a check, the PIN 482913 is pasted into the field](docs/images/real/copy-pin-copied.png) ```bash bigarrow start --element "PIN code" --role textfield --app "Google Chrome:Acme sign-in" --from right \ --color blue --border-color yellow --text-color yellow --text "Franz, copy & paste the PIN {{482913}} here" ``` ## What is this actually for? Fair question. Arrows have existed since roughly the Paleolithic. What changed: agents now do real work on your Mac, and sooner or later hit a step **only a human may do**, or one the human wants to learn. - **"Click Allow."** Permission prompts, OAuth consent, "Open with...?". The agent finds the button but must not, or cannot, press it. It can point. - **"Your turn."** 2FA, CAPTCHAs, passkeys, payments, signatures. It points, you decide, it continues. - **"Paste this."** A code, a URL, a command: on the sign with a [copy button](#copy--paste). - **"I need you, and you're making coffee."** `--say` reads the sign aloud. Your Mac will literally call you back to your desk. - **"Show me how."** Ask how to do something in Blender, and the agent points at each control in turn. A product tour, minus the product. - **Helping someone else.** On a parent's Mac or over a screen share, pointing beats "the button at the top, no, the other top". - **Demos and docs.** Highlight while recording, or render straight to a PNG with `--png`. - **Debugging coordinates.** Point at your Accessibility or Peekaboo coordinates and look. `--dry-run --json` says where it *would* point. Not a screen annotator, not a click bot, not a screenshot tool. It never clicks, types or captures. It only points. Deliberately. ## Install ```bash brew install franzenzenhofer/tap/bigarrow bigarrow install-skill # teaches Claude Code (~/.claude/skills) and Codex (~/.agents/skills) ``` From source: `swift build -c release` (Xcode 16+, macOS 14+), binary at `.build/release/bigarrow`. The binary is pure Swift; `scripts/` only records screenshots and runs tests. ## The three commands an agent needs ```bash bigarrow point --element "Allow" --app "System Settings" --text "Franz, click Allow" # by label bigarrow point --at 760,500 --text "Franz, click HERE" # by coordinate bigarrow start --window "Safari:Inbox" --text "This window" && bigarrow stop # until stopped ``` Every arrow ends by itself. Nobody has to clean up after an agent that forgot: | | | |---|---| | Time limit | `--duration 10` (`point` 8 s, `start` 300 s, `0` = no limit) | | Start and stop | `start` returns at once; `stop` (or `stop --all`) removes it | | The agent goes away | the arrow ends with the agent process that drew it (`CLAUDE_PID` or `BIGARROW_OWNER_PID`) | | The human answers | `bigarrow stop --hook` as a Claude Code `UserPromptSubmit` hook clears that session's arrows | | The human closes it | `--close-button` (opt-in) | Targets: `--at X,Y`, `--rect X,Y,W,H`, `--mouse`, `--window App[:title]`, `--element Label --app App`, `--peekaboo ID --snapshot see.json`. Coordinates are global top-left logical points, as Accessibility and Peekaboo report them; `--display N` makes them relative to one display. `--app App[:window or tab title]` (or `--window`) first brings that app, window or Chrome/Safari tab to the front, because pointing at a window hidden behind your terminal is a special kind of unhelpful. If another app covers the target later, the arrow hides until it is visible again. `--no-raise` opts out. `bigarrow elements --app X` lists what `--element` can match; `bigarrow doctor` shows permissions and displays. Every command takes `--json`. Exit codes: 0 ok, 2 bad input, 3 target not found, 4 permission missing. Agents love exit codes. Humans tolerate them. ## Looks It is an arrow, so we spent an unreasonable amount of time on how it looks. ![Big arrows with signs: click here, sign here, over here, you are here, type your name, read this first, no the other one, click Allow](docs/images/hero.png) ![every border style and colour option: default white border with shadow, white-black, black, close button, custom border and text colours](docs/images/looks.png) Six looks over white, macOS grey, dark, black, red and a busy web page: ![default, white-black, black, close button, custom colours and a black arrow, each over six backgrounds](docs/images/backgrounds.png) ![every style, shape, size and colour](docs/images/gallery.png)

extra.source_text:
An agent skill that builds award-caliber websites from one line
# /awwwards **An agent skill that builds award-caliber websites from one line.**

[Demo](#demo) · [Install](#install) · [Usage](#usage) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Limits](#limits)
``` > make me a portfolio, my name is Julio ``` That's the whole brief. The agent works as creative director, designer and creative developer in one, then hands back a site it has already checked in a real browser. ## Quick start ```bash npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g # optional: interactive isometric explainer figures npx skills add juliobsz/skills -g ``` Open a **new** agent session, then type `/awwwards` or just ask for a website. ## Demo [![Watch the demo on YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/BEcQoDs16IE/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://youtu.be/BEcQoDs16IE) Click on the thumbnail to watch the demo on YouTube ## Install Install with the [skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills). It runs through `npx`, so there's nothing to install first, and it detects your agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Copilot and more) and lets you pick. ```bash npx skills add juliobsz/skills -g ``` | Command | Result | |---|---| | `npx skills add juliobsz/skills -g -a claude-code` | Claude Code only (use `codex`, `cursor`… for others) | | `npx skills add juliobsz/skills` | This project only, instead of your user folder | | `npx skills add juliobsz/skills -g --copy` | Copy the files instead of linking them | | `npx skills update -g` | Update to the latest version | | `npx skills remove awwwards -g` | Uninstall | The CLI collects anonymous usage data. Set `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` or `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` to turn it off.
Claude Code plugin If you prefer Claude Code's plugin system, which updates the skill for you: ``` /plugin install awwwards --marketplace juliobsz/skills ``` On Claude Code before 2.1.275, run `/plugin marketplace add juliobsz/skills` and then `/plugin install awwwards@juliobsz`. The skill then runs as `/awwwards:awwwards`. Use the plugin or the skills CLI, not both, or the skill shows up twice.
Manual install Copy the `awwwards/` folder into your agent's skills directory, for example `~/.claude/skills/awwwards`. Any agent that reads `SKILL.md` skills can use it.
### Works with /anatomy [/anatomy](https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy) by wheresryan22 is an open-source skill for detailed, interactive isometric figures that explain an idea as a real physical object. Install it next to `/awwwards` and the site can get one "how it works" section built as a real explainer figure, styled to the site's palette and grid. ```bash npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g ``` It's optional. Without it, `/awwwards` builds that section another way, and tells you at the end when a figure would have helped. ### Requirements - **Node 22.20+** for the skills CLI. The helper scripts need Node 20+. - **Playwright** in the site's project for screenshots and the OG image, and **axe-core** for the accessibility pass. The skill installs both as dev dependencies when it needs them, and uses a Chromium you already have when it can. - **A model that can read images**, so the QA loop can look at its own screenshots. - **A Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare account** only if you want it to deploy.
Troubleshooting - **`/awwwards` isn't found.** Start a new session; agents read their skills folder at startup. Then run `npx skills list -g` to see where it was installed. - **It shows up twice.** You installed it two ways (for example the skills CLI and the plugin). Remove one with `npx skills remove awwwards -g` or `/plugin uninstall awwwards@juliobsz`. - **Installed into the wrong agent.** Name the target with `-a`, for example `-a codex`. - **Screenshots fail with "Playwright not found".** Run `npm i -D playwright` in the site's project. If it reports no Chromium, run `npx playwright install chromium` once.
## Why Ask an agent for "a portfolio" and you get the same site everyone gets: purple gradient, three cards, "elevate your brand". This skill replaces that default with a process. - **A concept that belongs to you.** Three ideas from different territories (your name, your craft, your place), scored on originality and fit. - **A real design system.** Palette by role, curated free fonts, grid and motion language, written to `DESIGN.md` and tested against a "genericness check". - **Motion with intent.** GSAP, Lenis and WebGL (OGL) where they earn their place, with one signature moment and everything else quiet. - **Real copy.** No lorem ipsum, fake awards or invented metrics. Anything made up is marked as a placeholder and listed at the end. - **Verified, not assumed.** A production build, a crawling audit and real-browser screenshots on desktop, mobile and reduced motion, scored against a rubric until every category hits 8/10. Its quality bar is the work that wins [Awwwards](https://www.awwwards.com) Site of the Day. The site doesn't need to be submitted anywhere; it just has to be that good. ## Usage Ask in one line and let the agent decide. It writes its assumptions down instead of running a questionnaire. ``` make me a portfolio, my name is Ana a site for my architecture studio in Lisbon, we do small houses launch page for a mechanical keyboard called Kestrel, it should feel insane redesign this landing page so it could win site of the day ``` Better input gives a better site. Your real name, what you do, where you are and two or three real projects let the concept come from your story instead of a placeholder. ## How it works | Phase | What happens | |---|---| | **Brief** | Infers who it's for, the audience and the site's job. Missing facts become written assumptions | | **Concept** | Three concepts from different territories (your name, your craft's materials, your place, how you work, a formal system), scored on originality and fit. The winner becomes a one-line idea with a signature moment | | **Art direction** | Palette by role, type pairing from a curated free-font library, grid, rhythm and motion language, all written to `DESIGN.md`. Then a "genericness test" kills anything an average model would have produced | | **Build** | Semantic HTML that looks finished with motion off. Then reveals, page transitions, a loader that tracks real loading, and the signature moment | | **QA loop** | Production build, a crawling audit (SEO, metadata, accessibility, weight, placeholder copy, AI-copy tells) and real-browser screenshots on desktop, mobile, reduced motion and mid-transition. It also measures LCP and CLS on a throttled phone, runs axe and tabs through every page. The agent reads every frame, a fresh critic subagent that never saw the plan scores the site against the rubric, and the agent fixes things until every category hits 8/10 | | **Ship** | OG image, favicon, sitemap, robots, then deploy to Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare (only after you confirm) | ### Stack - **Next.js** (App Router) by default, and for anything with app features. - **Astro** for content-only showcases where motion is the product: about 75 KB of JS against about 250 KB. - **Your stack** when you run it inside an existing project. All three use [GSAP](https://gsap.com) (every plugin is free now), [Lenis](https://lenis.dev) for smooth scroll and [OGL](https://github.com/oframe/ogl) for WebGL. The motion engine is framework-agnostic TypeScript, shipped as documented code instead of a template: it runs on one clock, reverts every effect on navigation, runs transitions in parallel with the next page loading, and keeps content visible without JavaScript or with reduced motion. ### Principles it won't break - One idea, one signature moment, everything else quiet. - Every frame works as a still poster before any motion is added. - The native cursor stays. Reduced motion gets a complete, calm site. Phones get a composed layout, not a shrunken one. - No fake awards, logos or metrics. No lorem ipsum. No em dashes or "elevate your brand" copy. - No purple gradients, glassmorphism or three-card grids unless the concept truly calls for them. ## Limits - **It takes a while.** A full run is concept, design system, build and several rounds of screenshots and fixes. Expect a long session and heavy token use, not a quick snippet. - **Results depend on the model.** It was built and tested with Claude Code and Codex. The concept and the visual QA are only as good as the model doing them. - **Content is yours to finish.** Without real projects, photos and copy, the site ships with clearly marked placeholders that you replace. - **8/10 is its own score.** The rubric keeps it honest, but you're the final judge. ## Standalone scripts The helpers in `awwwards/scripts/` work on any site, so you can use them on their own: ```bash node ~/.claude/skills/awwwards/scripts/audit.mjs https://your-site.com/ node ~/.claude/skills/awwwards/scripts/shoot.mjs https://your-site.com/ --crawl --nav ``` | Script | Does | |---|---| | `audit.mjs` | Crawl a build: SEO, a11y, weight, placeholders, AI-copy tells | | `shoot.mjs` | Screenshots of every page type: LCP/CLS on a throttled phone, FPS, overflow, tap targets, axe, keyboard focus, rest/hover pairs per pointer target, idle motion, transitions (needs Playwright; axe-core optional) | | `og.mjs` | Render the OG image from the live hero (needs Playwright) | | `font.mjs` | Self-host Fontshare / Google fonts (CSS or `next/font` output) | | `photos.mjs` | Contact sheets of free photos for marked placeholders | | `serve.mjs` | Static server for build output |

--- ## 截图 · Screenshots

--- ## 中文 **Win顺** 是 Windows 上免费开源的快速搜索启动器：连按两下 Ctrl 弹出搜索框，边打字边出结果。按文件名或拼音秒找文件，搜 Word、Excel、PDF 里的文字，打开应用和系统设置，还有剪贴板历史、对话框搜索、任务栏搜索框、插件和给 AI 用的 MCP 搜索。 它直接读 NTFS 主文件表（MFT）建索引，三百多万个文件几秒建好，增删改名实时跟上，**不用装 Everything**。不需要账号，不上传数据。界面有简体中文和英文。 ### 功能 #### 🔍 文件搜索 - **双击 Ctrl** 打开，再按一次或 `Esc` 关闭；三百多万个文件里搜一次只要几毫秒。 - **拼音和首字母**：`ndbg` → 年度报告，`baog` → 报告；多音字按常用读音。打错了同音字（年度报高）找不到时，自动按读音再找一遍。 - **搜整台电脑**：所有本地磁盘，U 盘可选（没收录的 U 盘插着时，列表末尾会提示你顺手搜一下它）；**NAS、内网共享文件夹（SMB）** 也能加进来一起搜，服务器关机时收录过的照样能搜到。 - **排序懂你**：自己的文件在前，系统目录、`node_modules` 在后，名字完全一样的最前。每行显示修改日期，`Ctrl+S` 在最匹配、最新、最早之间切换。不输入时列出最近打开或最近修改的文件。 - **数字键直达**：结果的图标上标着序号，`Ctrl+1`～`Ctrl+9` 打开第几行（也可改成 `Alt`）。 - **按类型找**：选中 **文件** 后，下面一排是文件夹、文档、图片、视频、压缩包等类型，`Tab` 依次切换；点 `+` 或在设置里自己加类型。 - **拖出去就能用**：结果直接拖进微信、邮件、资源管理器。 - **实时更新**：读 USN 变更日志，改名、新建、删除马上搜得到；拔 U 盘不会提示“设备正在使用”。 | 搜索语法 | 含义 | |---|---| | `报告 2024` | 每个词都要有（空格分隔，顺序不限）；也可以在所在文件夹的名字里 | | `ndbg`、`niandubaogao` | 拼音全拼、首字母，可以混用 | | `"年度 报告"` | 引号内作为整体 | | `!草稿`、`!node_modules\` | 排除文件名、排除文件夹 | | `*.pdf`、`报告?.docx` | 通配符 | | `ext:pdf,docx` | 只要这些扩展名 | | `项目\readme` | 在名字含“项目”的文件夹下 | | `tools/out/`、`D:\My Files\` | 路径直达：回车进去，列出里面的内容 | #### 📄 文件内容全文搜索 - 切到 **内容** 范围，搜文件里的文字，结果显示命中的那一行。 - **能搜的文件**： - 纯文本：txt、md、log、csv、json、代码等； - 文档：**Word、Excel、PowerPoint、PDF、WPS**，结果里显示第几页、第几张幻灯片或哪个表的第几行。 - **怎么找**：可以写多个词、用引号找整个短语，结果按相关度排。 - **编码和速度**：自动识别 UTF-8、UTF-16、GBK 编码；有内容索引，几十万个文件也很快。超过大小上限的、系统目录里的、类型没列出的文件默认不搜，搜完会告诉你各有几个，点一下就临时把它们也搜了。 - **安全**：文档由一个权限受限的独立进程读取。 #### 🚀 应用和系统设置 - **应用**：开始菜单里的所有应用都能搜，含 Microsoft Store 应用。名称、拼音、首字母（`vsc`）、程序名（`winword`）都行；`Ctrl+Shift+Enter` 以管理员身份运行。 - **系统设置**：约 1200 个 Windows 设置页和控制面板项。`shipeiqi`、“网卡”、`ncpa.cpl` 都能打开网络连接；另外补了组策略、磁盘管理、hosts、AppData 等开始菜单里没有的。 #### 🌐 网页搜索 · ⭐ 收藏夹 · 🧩 插件 - **网页搜索**：`baidu 天气`、`zhihu 显卡`、`jingdong 键盘`，关键词加空格就在那个网站上搜。 - 自带百度、必应、B 站、知乎、微博、抖音、小红书、淘宝、京东、翻译。 - 可以用 `%s` 网址添加自己的网站，图标、列表都能导入导出。 - **收藏夹**： - 右键“加入收藏夹”，不打字时排在最前； - 起个关键词，一打就开； - 收藏的文件夹按 `Tab` 进去接着搜。 - **插件**： - 随包的小工具：`= 1+2*3` 计算器、`12 inch to cm` 单位换算、`#ff8800` 颜色，还有时间戳、UUID、Base64、哈希； - `kill` 结束进程，`bm` 搜浏览器书签，`tr` 翻译； - 自己写插件：零代码的 `plugin.json`、任意语言的脚本或常驻进程都行，附 Python / PowerShell / C++ SDK； - 插件以普通权限、限内存运行。见 [docs/plugins.md](docs/plugins.md)。 #### 📂 “打开”“另存为”对话框 - **对话框旁的搜索框**：输入文件夹或文件名（拼音也行），回车，对话框直接转过去；网页上传文件、WPS 的对话框也认。 - **`Ctrl+G`**：转到资源管理器、Total Commander 或 Directory Opus 正在显示的文件夹，和 Listary 的同名快捷键一样。 - **不输入时**：列出打开着的文件夹、刚复制的路径、收藏和最近用过的文件夹。 - **自动转过去**：可以设成对话框一出现就转到文件管理器的文件夹，或者先停在上次的位置，从文件管理器切回来时再转。 #### 📋 剪贴板历史（代替 Win+V） - **记什么**：复制过的文字、图片、文件都记下来。 - **怎么打开**：`Win+V` 或自设的快捷键；开在输入光标旁，不抢焦点。 - **怎么粘贴**：双击或 `Enter` 粘贴，`Shift+Enter` 粘贴为纯文本，`Alt+1`～`9` 直接粘贴第几条（序号标在图标上）。 - **能搜**：拼音搜索，`@wx` 只看微信里复制的；**图片里的字也能搜**（Windows 自带的文字识别 OCR，在本机，不联网）。 - **预览**：全文、大图、颜色值的 HEX / RGB / HSL。 - **拖出图片**：按住一张图片拖到文件夹里，就存成 PNG 文件。 - **整理**：固定、分组、多选按顺序合并粘贴，钉住后可以一条接一条地往表格里填。 - **隐私**：密码管理器复制的密码不记录，历史只存在本机。 #### 🔎 任务栏搜索框（代替 Windows 搜索） - 在 Windows 11 任务栏上放 Win顺 自己的搜索框（Windows 10 是固定一个按钮），结果从任务栏上方滑出。 - 可以像 Windows 自带的搜索框一样放在开始按钮右边，图标往右让出位置（设置里打开，默认关）。 - 可以接管 `Win+S`，开始菜单里打字也用 Win顺 搜。 #### 🤖 AI 助手（MCP） - **能做什么**：Win顺 是一个 MCP 服务器，AI 能用它搜文件名、文件内容和最近修改的文件。 - **怎么连**：Claude Desktop、Claude Code、Cursor、VS Code 在设置里一键连接。 - **安全**： - 默认只读，只看得到 AI 客户端自己有权限看的文件； - 可以设不让 AI 看到的文件夹； - 每次调用都有记录。 #### 🎨 外观和设置 - **外观**：浅色、深色跟随系统，Windows 11 云母（Mica）效果和圆角；图标在 150% 缩放下也清晰。 - **设置**：可以搜索（`Ctrl+F`，`kjj` 找到“快捷键”），改了立即生效。 - **更新**：有新版本时在托盘提醒，Win顺 不会自己下载、替换程序文件。 | 按键 | 作用 | |---|---| | 双击 `Ctrl` | 打开 / 关闭搜索框（可另设组合键，如 `Alt+Space`） | | `Enter` / `Ctrl+Enter` / `Ctrl+Shift+Enter` | 打开 / 打开所在文件夹 / 以管理员身份运行 | | `Ctrl+C` / `Ctrl+Shift+C` | 复制文件 / 复制路径 | | `Ctrl+1`～`Ctrl+9` | 打开第几行（图标上的数字） | | `Tab` / `Shift+Tab` | 切换范围：全部 / 文件 / 内容；在 **文件** 里 `Tab` 切换类型 | | `Ctrl+S` | 最匹配 → 最新在前 → 最早在前 | | `Ctrl+G`（对话框里） | 转到文件管理器正在显示的文件夹 | | `Win+V` / `Win+S`（设置里打开后） | 剪贴板历史 / 任务栏上方的搜索框 | ### 下载安装 1. 到 [Releases 页面](https://github.com/LingCore/WinShun/releases/latest) 下载 `WinShun-版本号-x64-setup.exe`，双击安装。Windows 提示“已保护你的电脑”时，点 **更多信息 → 仍要运行**（还没有代码签名证书）。 2. 装完托盘里出现 Win顺 的图标，索引几秒就建好。连按两下 Ctrl 开始搜索。 3. 升级时运行新的安装程序，设置和索引都保留。卸载在 Windows 的“设置 → 应用”里。 不想安装的话，下载 `WinShun-版本号-x64-portable.zip`，解压到任意文件夹，运行里面的 `WinShun.exe` 就行。设置和索引和安装版放在同一个地方（`%APPDATA%\WinShun`、`%LOCALAPPDATA%\WinShun`），不在解压的文件夹里；升级时用新版的文件夹换掉旧的。 系统要求：Windows 10 或 11，64 位。 ### 为什么需要管理员权限 - **为什么要**：读 NTFS 主文件表（MFT）和 USN 变更日志，才能几秒建好索引、实时跟上改动。开机自启用的是最高权限的计划任务，所以开机不弹 UAC。 - **打开的东西仍是普通权限**：从 Win顺 打开的文件和应用都以普通权限运行，只有 `Ctrl+Shift+Enter` 才以管理员身份运行。 ### 常见问题 **和 Everything、Listary 有什么区别？** Win顺 自己建索引，不用装 Everything。文件名、拼音、应用和文件内容在一个框里搜，针对中文做了优化。对话框里有和 Listary 一样的 `Ctrl+G` 和搜索框，但不嵌进资源管理器窗口。 **双击 Ctrl 和别的软件冲突？** Listary、PowerToys 的“查找鼠标”默认也用双击 Ctrl，关掉其中一边就行。也可以在 Win顺 里改用别的组合键。游戏全屏、藏起鼠标时，Win顺 默认不响应双击 Ctrl。 **AutoHotkey 改的键在 Win顺 里不起作用？** Win顺 以管理员身份运行，Windows 不让普通权限的程序拦截发给它的按键。用 AutoHotkey 的 UI Access 模式，或以管理员身份运行脚本。 **占多少内存？索引能不放 C 盘吗？** - **内存**：每 100 万个文件约 30 MB，用着的时候整个程序一般 120～140 MB；不用它一分钟后，任务管理器里降到十几 MB。 - **索引位置**：在设置 → 高级 → 索引位置里，可以移到其他内置硬盘。 **收费吗？会上传数据吗？** 完全免费，MIT 开源。只在两种时候联网：到 GitHub 检查新版本（可以关掉），第一次显示某个网页搜索时取一次那个网站的图标。索引和历史只存在本机（`%LOCALAPPDATA%\WinShun`）。 ### 反馈 遇到问题或有建议，欢迎在 [Issues](https://github.com/LingCore/WinShun/issues) 里提出。 ### 从源码编译 需要 Visual Studio 2022（“使用 C++ 的桌面开发”）、Qt 6.8 或更新版本（推荐 6.12，MSVC 2022 64 位套件）、CMake 3.25+ 和 Ninja。 ```powershell ./scripts/build.ps1 # 编译 + 运行单元测试 ./scripts/build.ps1 -QtDir C:\Qt\6.12.0\msvc2022_64 # 指定 Qt（默认用 QTDIR 或 C:\Qt 下最新的版本） ./scripts/build.ps1 -Deploy # 生成可分发的文件夹 dist\WinShun ./scripts/release.ps1 # 打包安装程序和 SHA256SUMS.txt（需要 Inno Setup 6.5+）；加 -Publish 发布到 GitHub ``` 也可以用 Qt Creator 或 VS Code（CMake Tools）打开，预设见 `CMakePresets.json`。源码结构和设计见 [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md)，踩过的坑见 [docs/pitfalls.md](docs/pitfalls.md)。 --- ## English **WinShun** (Win顺, "Windows made smooth") is a free, open-source search launcher for Windows. Press Ctrl twice and a search bar pops up, with results as you type: - find files and folders by name or by pinyin; - search the text inside Word, Excel and PDF files; - launch apps and open Windows settings. It also brings a clipboard history, a search bar for file dialogs, a taskbar search box, plugins and an MCP server for AI assistants. It reads the NTFS master file table (MFT) directly, indexing three million files in a few seconds and following every change live: **no Everything install needed**. It needs no account and uploads nothing. The interface comes in English and Simplified Chinese. Screenshots: [above](#screenshots). ### Features

# Model Pulse

Daily download history, likes and derivative families for every model on the Hugging Face Hub, going back to July 2024.

- Look up any model: `?model=org/name`
- Compare up to five models on one chart
- See how much of a model's reach comes from its quantizations, fine-tunes, adapters and merges
- Galaxy: every model built on a base model, drawn as a galaxy (`?view=galaxy`)
- Wrapped: any author's last 12 months on the Hub in six cards (`?view=wrapped`)
- Weekly rankings: most downloaded, fastest growing, new breakouts, biggest families, organizations
- A README badge with monthly downloads and a sparkline, updated daily

Data comes from daily snapshots of [cfahlgren1/hub-stats](https://huggingface.co/datasets/cfahlgren1/hub-stats), compiled into [modelpulse/model-pulse-data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/modelpulse/model-pulse-data). An independent project, not affiliated with Hugging Face.

Every model also has its own page at [modelpulse.ifsp.dev](https://modelpulse.ifsp.dev), for example [Qwen/Qwen3-8B](https://modelpulse.ifsp.dev/model/Qwen/Qwen3-8B).

Made by **Tardelli Stekel** ([@tardellirs](https://huggingface.co/tardellirs), [stekel.ifsp.dev](https://stekel.ifsp.dev/)).

extra.candidate_title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
extra.source_text: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output. A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.” Cut once, measure twice To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026. To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations. If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code. Credit: Chen and Stratton If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code. Credit: Chen and Stratton In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction). The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write. In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms. Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era. Credit: Chen and Stratton Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era. Credit: Chen and Stratton While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work. AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems. For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies.
